overview: The HC-SR04 measures distance the way a bat does: it sends out a short burst of ultrasonic sound (well above human hearing) and times how long it takes the echo to bounce back off an object. That time-of-flight is converted into a distance using the speed of sound. It's the most common 'first sensor' in robotics because it's cheap, simple to wire (just 4 pins), and gives genuinely useful, fairly accurate readings for hobbyist-level obstacle detection. It belongs to the family of time-of-flight distance sensors, alongside sharper but pricier alternatives like laser (ToF) sensors.

specifications.echoOutputSignal: TTL pulse, width proportional to distance

pinMap.name: VCC
pinMap.function: Power input for the sensor's onboard circuitry and ultrasonic transducers.
pinMap.currentLimit: ~15 mA typical, higher during the ultrasonic pulse burst
pinMap.gotcha: This sensor is designed for 5V logic; running it directly off a 3.3V board's power rail generally gives unreliable range or won't work at all.

pinMap.name: TRIG
pinMap.function: Input pin. Sending a 10-microsecond HIGH pulse here tells the sensor to emit an 8-pulse ultrasonic burst at 40kHz.
pinMap.gotcha: The pulse must be at least 10 microseconds — shorter pulses are commonly ignored, and this is the #1 reason a first attempt reads all zeros.

pinMap.name: ECHO
pinMap.function: Output pin. Goes HIGH the instant the ultrasonic burst is sent and stays HIGH until the echo returns — the HIGH duration in microseconds is what you convert into distance.
pinMap.gotcha: This pin outputs a full 5V signal. If wired directly into a 3.3V-only board input (e.g., certain ESP32/STM32 pins), it can damage that pin — use a voltage divider or level shifter in that case.

pinMap.name: GND
pinMap.function: Ground reference, shared with the controlling microcontroller.
pinMap.gotcha: Must be common with the microcontroller's ground or the ECHO timing reading will be meaningless.

useCases.title: Obstacle-avoiding robot
useCases.scenario: Mount the sensor facing forward on a wheeled robot; when measured distance drops below a threshold, stop or turn away from the obstacle.

useCases.title: Parking sensor simulation
useCases.scenario: Combine with a buzzer or LED bar that beeps/lights faster as an object gets closer, mimicking a car parking sensor.

useCases.title: Non-contact liquid level indicator
useCases.scenario: Mount facing down into an open tank to estimate fill level from the distance to the liquid surface (works best with still, non-foaming liquids).

useCases.title: Gesture-triggered interaction (theremin-style)
useCases.scenario: Map real-time distance readings to a musical pitch or LED brightness for a hand-controlled interactive display.

useCases.title: Automatic bin lid
useCases.scenario: Detect a hand approaching the bin and trigger a servo to open the lid, closing it again after a delay.

oftenConfusedWith: IR distance sensors (shorter range, less accurate on dark/reflective surfaces, but faster and no dead cone)
PIR motion sensors (detect motion/heat, not distance)
oftenUpgradedTo: VL53L0X / VL53L1X laser (ToF) distance sensors (higher precision, narrower beam, I2C interface)

beginnerMistakes: Aiming the sensor at soft or angled surfaces (fabric, foam, sharply angled walls) — sound gets absorbed or deflected away instead of bouncing back, giving no reading or a wildly wrong one.
Forgetting the minimum range (~2cm) — objects closer than that are often missed entirely.
Not accounting for the ~15-degree cone — the sensor can 'see' objects off to the side that aren't directly in front, confusing obstacle-avoidance logic.
Polling it faster than the sensor can settle (recommended ~60ms between readings), causing echo readings to overlap and return garbage values.
